title: The Educated Barbarian: Hagakure analysis (part. 2)
summary: Second part of his Hagakure reading, covering accepting death, rehearsing mortality, decision making, ego and seeking advice from others. He ties the passages to visualization before heavy lifts, working past bad genetics and total commitment to a goal.
claims: Everyone should be able to state without hesitation what their way of life is; hesitating shows you never seriously thought about it
The answer can differ from man to man and that diversity is fine, but you cannot falter in giving your own
If you cannot say clearly what you are doing with your life, you are blindly going through the motions
Accepting death as part of daily life exists in both Eastern and Western thought; he reads nihilism as: since we all die, be at ease with it and do everything you can before it comes
Facing death like a man does not mean letting yourself be killed; it means not living in anxiety fighting an inevitable end
Intellectualising running from danger as a small choice is still cowardice; choosing self-preservation is your right, but do not lie to yourself about it
He resonates with Yamamoto's hatred of hypocrisy: hold strong beliefs and live by them
Rehearsing your death means being aware of your mortality and at peace with it; people who never do this panic and lose their dignity when death approaches
Accepting mortality makes you appreciate life more and want to be healthy and spend time with loved ones
Repeatedly visualizing a stressful situation is practice that builds confidence; anxious people let the thought occupy them but never attack it
Before a heavy deadlift session, spend the day visualizing yourself lifting the weight; a lift with a 50 percent chance of failure can become a sure thing
Men differ in natural talent, wealth, looks and muscle-building genetics; denying that is refusing reality
Faced with bad genetics, poverty or bad health you can throw a pity party or work; work is always the better option
Spend little time on big decisions and think a lot about small recurring ones, because small things repeat and the thinking pays off later
Coin-flip trick: imagine flipping a coin for a big decision; the side you hope it lands on is the decision you already want
Overthinking in a life-or-death moment lets the ego take over and find a thousand reasons not to act selflessly
Online IQ culture that belittles others is misguided: emotional intelligence can matter more and intelligence is contextual
However smart you are, you have limits that can be overcome by listening to others; people who think they know everything give bad advice
The way means staying humble and learning every day; stop learning and you stagnate
Modern society still loves confidence deep down but wears a social mask that labels it arrogance
A woman who says up front she dislikes muscular men is projecting an image of being hard to get; muscle is a broadly attractive biological trait
Samurai were community members serving a lord, not Westernised lone wolves; taking advice shows you are rooted like a big tree
Society still scorns men who admit weakness or try things; those who never try lash out from low self-worth, so be true to yourself and share anyway
Someone fully committed to a goal, willing to sacrifice easy pleasures like five hours of TV for it, carries a magnetic energy and inspires others
Being truly willing to go all in already puts you above 95 percent of people, who never follow through
